humanities_role_explanation: Humanities subjects (history, philosophy, law, religion, logic, morality) are 13 of 57 tasks, but the benchmark is a general multitask knowledge test; items are exam-style multiple-choice questions measuring general world knowledge and problem solving, not humanistic interpretive competence. The humanities are one supercategory among STEM, social science and other.
benchmark_modalities_explanation: Text-only multiple-choice questions; the paper explicitly designs the benchmark in a text-only format.
analytical_tasks_explanation: Four-option multiple-choice questions across 57 subjects, testing declarative knowledge and problem solving. Humanities items include inference from primary-source passages (Act of Supremacy, Paine, Bismarck), legal scenario application, formal logic, logical fallacies, and moral scenarios (ETHICS) for predicting 'widespread moral intuitions'. The paper also analyses calibration (confidence vs accuracy, RMS calibration error). Most humanities items test recognition of textbook or exam knowledge rather than deep interpretation.

general_purpose_benchmark.note: Broad multitask benchmark with 57 tasks across STEM, humanities, social sciences and other.

evaluates_generative_llm.note: GPT-3 (Small, Medium, Large, X-Large) few-shot and zero-shot; UnifiedQA; fine-tuned RoBERTa, ALBERT, GPT-2.

quantitative_metrics.note: Classification accuracy and RMS calibration error.

summary: The paper introduces MMLU, a 57-subject multiple-choice benchmark of exam-style questions spanning STEM, humanities, social sciences and other fields, evaluated in zero-shot and few-shot settings. The largest GPT-3 reaches 43.9% few-shot accuracy, far below estimated expert-level performance, with lopsided subject performance and poor calibration.
key_findings: GPT-3 X-Large few-shot reaches 43.9% average accuracy (40.8% on humanities); UnifiedQA reaches 48.9% (45.6% on humanities). Smaller GPT-3 models are near random (25%). Zero-shot GPT-3 is about 37.7%. Performance is lopsided; models do poorly on Professional Law and Moral Scenarios and on calculation-heavy subjects. Confidence can be up to 24% off accuracy. Expert-level accuracy is estimated at about 89.8%.
facets_explanation: Questions were manually collected by graduate and undergraduate students from freely available online sources such as GRE and USMLE practice questions, AP-style exams, undergraduate course questions and Oxford University Press reader questions, so the answer keys come from existing assessment material. Most items require external knowledge not in the question. Each item has one correct option, and the paper does not discuss disagreement between defensible readings.
results_explanation: Table 1 reports 'UnifiedQA 45.6 56.6 40.2 54.6 48.9' (average 48.9) and 'GPT-3 X-Large (few-shot) 40.8 50.4 36.7 48.8 43.9'. Zero-shot GPT-3 X-Large is 'about 37.7%' versus 43.9% few-shot, a gap of about 6-7 points (rounded up to 7). The paper estimates expert-level accuracy at 'approximately 89.8%', so the gap to the best model (48.9) is 41 points (89.8-48.9=40.9, rounded). Unspecialized MTurk humans score 34.5%.

humanities_role.quote: The benchmark covers 57 subjects across STEM, the humanities, the social sciences, and more.

dataset_size.quote: We collected 15908 questions in total, which we split into a few-shot development set, a validation set, and a test set.

primary_evaluation_setting.quote: we assess pretrained models in a zero-shot, few-shot, or transfer setting

gold_beyond_stimulus.quote: To succeed at our test, future models should be well-rounded, possess extensive world knowledge, and develop expert-level problem solving ability.

answer_multiplicity.quote: we instead create a simple-to-evaluate test that measures classification accuracy on multiple choice questions.

reported_format_gap_kind.quote: Notably, zero-shot performance is only somewhat lower than 5-shot accuracy.
